def: Knowledge comes from experience, and decisions are made on what is observed. Together with lean thinking, this is what Scrum is founded on. In practice it means you only get to plan forward using what has actually happened.

The emergent process and work must be visible to those performing the work as well as those receiving it. Low transparency in the artifacts leads to decisions that diminish value and increase risk. Transparency enables inspection.

The artifacts and progress toward agreed goals are examined frequently and diligently to detect undesirable variances or problems. Inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful. Inspection enables adaptation.
When something has drifted outside acceptable limits, the process or the product is adjusted, as soon as possible. Inspection without adaptation is considered pointless.

One Scrum Master, one Product Owner, and Developers. No sub-teams and no hierarchies. Typically 10 or fewer people, cross-functional and self-managing. The entire Scrum Team is accountable for creating a valuable, useful Increment every Sprint.

Accountable for maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and for effective Product Backlog management. One person, not a committee. May delegate the work, but remains accountable.

Accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide, and for the Scrum Team's effectiveness. A true leader who serves the Scrum Team and the wider organization. Not a manager and not a secretary.

The people on the Scrum Team committed to creating any aspect of a usable Increment each Sprint. They create the Sprint Backlog, instill quality by adhering to the Definition of Done, adapt their plan daily toward the Sprint Goal, and hold each other accountable. They also size the work.

Who answers for an outcome. Distinct from responsibility, which is who does the task. A Product Owner may hand the writing of backlog items to someone else, and is still the one who answers for the backlog. The exam leans on this distinction constantly.
The Scrum Team internally decides who does what, when, and how. This replaced the 2017 Guide's term self-organizing, and it is broader: it covers the how as well as the who.
The team members between them have all the skills necessary to create value each Sprint, without waiting on a group outside the team.
A fixed-length event of one month or less, and the container for all the other events. A new Sprint starts immediately after the previous one concludes. Each Sprint may be considered a short project.

Opens the Sprint. Covers three topics: why this Sprint is valuable, what can be Done, and how the chosen work gets done. The whole Scrum Team collaborates. Timeboxed to a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint.

A 15-minute event for the Developers, to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog. Same time and place each working day. The Product Owner attends only as a Developer, and only if actively working on Sprint Backlog items.

The Scrum Team and key stakeholders inspect the outcome of the Sprint and collaborate on what to do next. A working session, not a presentation. The second to last event of the Sprint. Maximum four hours for a one-month Sprint.

The Scrum Team plans ways to increase quality and effectiveness, inspecting individuals, interactions, processes, tools, and its Definition of Done. It concludes the Sprint. Maximum three hours for a one-month Sprint.
An emergent, ordered list of what is needed to improve the product, and the single source of work undertaken by the Scrum Team. It is never finished.

Breaking down and further defining items into smaller, more precise ones, adding detail such as description, order and size. An ongoing activity, not an event. Nothing in the Guide says when or how often it happens.

Putting the Product Backlog into a single sequence. This is the Product Owner's call. Note the word: the Guide says ordered, not prioritized. Five items can share a priority label, but only one can be next.

The long-term objective for the Scrum Team, describing a future state of the product. It lives in the Product Backlog, and it is that artifact's commitment. The team must fulfill or abandon one objective before taking on the next.
A vehicle to deliver value. It has a clear boundary, known stakeholders, and well-defined users or customers. It could be a service, a physical product, or something more abstract.

The Sprint Goal (why), the Product Backlog items selected for the Sprint (what), and an actionable plan for delivering the Increment (how). A plan by and for the Developers, updated throughout the Sprint.

The single objective for the Sprint, and the Sprint Backlog's commitment. Crafted by the whole Scrum Team during Sprint Planning, and finalized before Sprint Planning ends. It is a commitment by the Developers, and it gives them flexibility about the exact work.

A concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal, additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified. It must be usable. Multiple Increments may be created in a Sprint, and one may be delivered before the Sprint ends.

A formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product, and the Increment's commitment. Work that does not meet it cannot be released, or even presented at the Sprint Review.
src: Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done

def: Each artifact carries exactly one, to reinforce empiricism and focus. Product Backlog carries the Product Goal, Sprint Backlog carries the Sprint Goal, Increment carries the Definition of Done. This pairing is heavily tested.

Anyone outside the Scrum Team with an interest in the product. Not a Scrum accountability. Stakeholders are invited to the Sprint Review, and anyone wanting to change the Product Backlog does so by trying to convince the Product Owner.
src: Scrum Guide 2020, Sprint Review and Product Owner

def: A Sprint may be cancelled if the Sprint Goal becomes obsolete. Only the Product Owner has the authority to do it. Rare in practice, and a favourite exam question.

Scrum.org's framework for measuring value, built on four Key Value Areas: Current Value, Unrealized Value, Time-to-Market, and Ability to Innovate. Official Scrum.org material and in scope for PSPO I, but it is not part of the Scrum Guide.

A common format for expressing a backlog item, usually as: as a WHO, I want WHAT, so that WHY. Widely useful, taught in CSPO, and completely absent from the Scrum Guide. The Guide asks only that items be created and clearly communicated.
A common way to size items and to gauge how much a team gets through. Neither appears in the Scrum Guide. The Guide says only that the Developers who will do the work are responsible for sizing.

A checklist some teams require before an item may enter a Sprint. Not in the Scrum Guide, and a common wrong answer. The Guide says items that can be Done within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection.
